title: Bidriware
description: Bidriware is the signature metalcraft of Bidar: a zinc-and-copper alloy inlaid with hammered silver and blackened with a paste of soil from the Bidar fort, made the same way for more than five centuries.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Bidar · Since c. 1500

items.value: Zinc-and-copper alloy, inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire
A paste of soil from the Bidar fort
Registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) of India

blocks.intro: Bidriware is the signature metalcraft of Bidar, made the same way for more than five centuries. A vessel of zinc-and-copper alloy is cast, scored with a steel point, inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire, and then dipped in a paste of soil from the Bidar fort that turns the alloy a deep matte black — leaving the silver inlay untouched and gleaming against it. No other metalwork looks like it.

sections.sub: Casting, scoring, inlay, and the blackening paste unique to Bidar
body: The craft takes its name from Bidar, the only place it has ever been made. A vessel is cast in an alloy of zinc and copper, its surface scored with a steel point in a pattern, then inlaid with hammered silver and brass wire set into the scored lines. The vessel is finally dipped in a paste made from soil taken from within the Bidar fort itself, which reacts with the alloy to turn it a deep matte black — while leaving the silver, untouched by the reaction, standing out bright against it.<cite data-ref="michell-zebrowski-1999"></cite>

sections.sub: Still practised by Bidar's karigars, and protected as a Geographical Indication
body: Bidriware remains in production in Bidar today, carried on by the same families of karigars who have practised it for generations. It is registered as a Geographical Indication (GI) of India, recognition of a craft that, despite its fame across the Deccan and beyond, has never been successfully replicated anywhere else — the blackening reaction depends on the particular soil of the Bidar fort itself.

references.text: George Michell & Mark Zebrowski, Architecture and Art of the Deccan Sultanates (The New Cambridge History of India I.7), Cambridge University Press, 1999.
